title: How do you keep AI-generated worlds consistent? I'm building a life sim and statefulness is the biggest challenge
author: lukinator644
selftext:
I'm working on Altworld, a browser-based AI life sim. Players can pitch a world, create a character, and advance turn-by-turn with freeform actions. The AI tracks consequences, saves, and NPCs. That part is tricky.

Getting the blacksmith to remember you trashed his shop three turns ago isn't just a prompt tweak. The LLM alone won't hold that across a long session. Right now I'm leaning on structured summaries injected back into context, but the balance between detail and token budget is delicate.

Curious what approaches others are trying. Are you embedding world state, using vector DBs, or something else?

comments.author: orblabs
comments.body: That is the case for a database. You keep track of per character interactions and then assemble context querying the database when needed again. Not all there is to it but should give you the right input towards handling that. (I've been building something vaguely similar for the last way too many months... ) Best luck and have fun working on it

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
Yeah, one of the things that was a huge game changer for me in the way i thought about it was realizing that the ai is autosummarizing the chat we are having, already. 

The llm is stateless, that when i chat to it, behind the scenes it’s creating it’s own summary of our conversation and feeding it back into the prompt that i’m seeing thus creating the context window. 

So essentially, I’m experimenting with automated prompt crafting, in my case, through unity, where the data for the context window is stored in unity and it’s crafting a new context window with every prompt. 

One of the ideas i’m going to mess around with is using a very simple llm along with traditional code, to decide which parts of the backstory/npc data file to pull, and a better llm to actually craft the message. 

But that is theoretical at this point.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
You're falling into the "use llm for everything" trap. Traditional database frameworks will serve you far better here for consistent data tracking. It requires you to build and maintain complex systems upfront, however.

Also don't fuck with vector DBs for something like this. Way too much extraneous data to deal with. Vector DBs can be used for these purposes, but they're the lazy man's way to avoid creating detailed relational DBs. Sit down and map out a well thought out system with clear storage and recall and you won't need the nebulous queries of a vector DB which would otherwise have... inconsistent results.

replies.author: orblabs
replies.body: Why not both 😄  I have a solid relational db linked to a vector db too, baed on the needs i can exploit one or the other or both.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: You CAN have both. I personally have never found a use for a vector DB in situations where I'm explicitly defining byte-sized data containers. I break down the  important data into relational pieces before storing, and use an exhaustive set of triggers to call different pieces when needed to assemble the important data. I think larger, SOTA models would be better equipped to handle vector data since they can parse through thousands or tens of thousands of unnecessary add-in tokens from a vector call, but as I don't find them profitable to work with and instead use smaller llms to drive game processes, they're far more vulnerable to content bloat and perform exponentially better with sharp, highly tuned requests.
